name: Akkud
title: Descendant of David through Zerubbabel
summary: Akikud is listed in 1 Chronicles as one of seven sons of Eljoenai, and thus belongs to the Davidic royal line through the lineage of Zerubbabel. As part of the post-exilic generation, he represents an important link in the royal genealogy following the return from Babylon. The precise recording of his name among Eljoenai's sons testifies to the Jewish community's dedication to preserving genealogical records of David's descendants, a practice with deep messianic significance in light of God's covenant promises of an eternal throne for David's offspring.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in David's genealogy
keyEvents.description: Akkud is listed as one of the seven sons of Eljoenai, a descendant of David through Zerubbabel, in the post-exilic genealogy in 1 Chronicles.

keyEvents.title: Part of the Davidic lineage after the exile
keyEvents.description: Through his father Eljoenai, Akikud is connected to Zerubbabel, who led the Jews back from the Babylonian exile. The recording of his name in the genealogies testifies to faithfulness in preserving the royal line of David and to God's faithfulness to covenant promises of an eternal throne for David's descendants.

versions.summary: Akikud is mentioned in 1 Chronicles as a descendant of King David through Zerubbabel. He belongs to the post-exilic generation of David's royal lineage. His significance lies primarily in his place in the messianic line.
versions.title: Descendant of Zerubbabel
versions.reason: [major] Ahikud is not described as a 'leader' anywhere in the Bible. He is only mentioned as a descendant of David in a genealogy. The role should be changed to something more precise, such as 'descendant of David'.; [minor] The claim that Ahikud has a place in 'the messianic lineage' is somewhat imprecise. Jesus's messianic lineage in Matthew and Luke does not explicitly go through Eljoenai/Ahikud. He belongs to the Davidic royal line, but calling it 'the messianic lineage' can be misleading.; [minor] The second keyEvent ('Part of the royal lineage') refers to a very large number of verses (1 Chron 3:1-5, 10, 15-24), which is excessively broad. The reference should be limited to the most relevant verses for Ahikud's connection.; [minor] Four keyEvents for a person mentioned in only one verse (1 Chron 3:24) are excessive. The events overlap heavily with each other and can be consolidated.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. A person like Ahikud deserves at least one footnote about the meaning of the name, the Davidic lineage after the exile, or textual critical questions surrounding 1 Chron 3:22-24.

versions.summary: Akikud is mentioned in 1 Chronicles as a son of Eljoenai and a descendant of King David through Zerubbabel. He belongs to the post-exilic generation of David's royal lineage. His significance lies primarily in his role in preserving the Davidic line after returning from the Babylonian exile.
versions.title: Descendant of David through Zerubbabel
versions.reason: [major] According to 1 Chr 3:24, Eljoenai has seven sons: Hodavja, Eljasib, Pelaja, Akkub, Johanan, Delaja and Anani. The list omits 'anani' and includes 'akkub' as a sibling, but Akikud himself is likely identical to Akkub (as noted in the footnotes). If Akikud = Akkub, then Akkub should not appear as a sibling. Alternatively, if Akikud is a separate person from Akkub, Anani should still be included. Here, 'akkub' should be removed from the list of siblings (since Akikud is probably a variant of Akkub) and 'anani' added.; [minor] The second key event includes verses 19, 21 and 23, which do not directly mention Akikud. Verse 19 concerns the sons of Zerubbabel, while verses 21 and 23 concern intermediate generations. This is acceptable as context but could be clarified further.; [minor] The footnote on textual critical issues is labeled 'theological', but its content deals primarily with textual criticism and manuscript traditions. 'Linguistic' would have been more appropriate, though a linguistic footnote already exists. Alternatively, 'other' fits better.; [minor] The summary is good but could be strengthened with a brief theological reflection on the messianic line, since the preservation of the Davidic lineage has messianic implications.

versions.summary: Akikud is mentioned in 1 Chronicles as one of the sons of Eljoenai, a descendant of King David through Zerubbabel. He belongs to the post-exilic generation of the Davidic royal family. The recording of his name in the genealogy testifies to the Jewish community's care in preserving the Davidic line after returning from Babylon, which has messianic significance in light of God's covenant promises to David.
versions.title: Descendant of David through Zerubbabel
versions.reason: [major] According to 1 Chr 3:24, the sons of Eljoenai are Hodavja, Eljasib, Pelaja, Akkub (Akikud), Johanan, Delaja and Anani. The order in the sibling list should reflect the biblical sequence, with 'hodavja' first, followed by 'eljasib', 'pelaja', 'johanan', 'delaja', 'anani'. The current order appears correct, but it is worth noting that some manuscripts show slight variations in the sequence.; [minor] The second key event includes verses 19, 21 and 23 from 1 Chr 3, but Akikud is not directly mentioned in these verses. Verse 19 concerns the sons of Zerubbabel, while verses 21 and 23 concern other generations. It may be misleading to include these as a separate key event with these specific verses. It would be better to limit the reference to the most relevant verses or clarify that these are contextual verses.; [minor] The summary is well phrased, but to distinguish it further from earlier versions, it could be strengthened by adding a brief clarification that Akikud is one of seven named sons, as well as emphasizing the genealogical context more clearly.

footnotes.text: The name Akikud (Hebrew: עַקּוּב, likely a variant of Akkub) may mean 'cunning' or 'one who holds fast.' The form of the name varies among different Hebrew manuscripts and translations, and there is discussion among textual critics about the relationship between Akikud and the more familiar form Akkub.

The genealogy in 1 Chron 3:17–24 is one of the most important sources for the Davidic royal line after the Babylonian exile. It shows that the Jewish community continued to keep careful track of David's descendants, even after the monarchy had ended. The number of generations after Zerubbabel has been a subject of debate and has implications for dating the books of Chronicles.

There are textual critical questions related to 1 Chron 3:22–24, especially regarding how the genealogical links should be counted. The Septuagint has some differences from the Hebrew Masoretic text in this passage, which affects the reconstruction of the exact lineage from Zerubbabel to Akikud.

The preservation of David's line through generations after the exile has theological significance, as it points toward the fulfillment of God's covenant with David (2 Sam 7:12–16). The careful recording of descendants like Akikud testifies to the belief that God's promises of an eternal Davidic throne remained valid.

In rabbinic tradition, the genealogies in Chronicles have been seen as important for establishing messianic claims. The preservation of such detailed lists in the post-exilic period reflects a living expectation of a coming Davidic Messiah, and the names in these lists were treated with great reverence.
